title: What Fell From the Tree
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hookLine: every time the hunter drew his bow, leaves and water fell on a stone he couldn't see
carry: ashutosha: shiva is pleased by a leaf and water
tomorrow: the deer promised to come back. did they?
last: JAPA: THE NAME, AND THE NEXT BEAD.

cards: Back to the hunter, Gurudruha, up in the bilva tree. Every time a deer came down to the pool, he shifted on his branch and pulled back his bow.
And every time he moved, a few bilva leaves shook loose, and water slopped from the pot he'd brought. Down they went in the dark, onto a stone he couldn't see. It was a Shiva linga.
Watch after watch, the Shiva Purana says, his fidgeting became worship: water poured, bilva laid down, all night long, by a man who only wanted dinner.

teach.b: This is why the plate looks the way it does on Shivaratri.
Go to a Shiva temple that night and look at what people carry: a little pot of water or milk, a few bilva leaves, three to a stem, a flower from the roadside. Nothing that costs much.
The water is poured over the linga; the pouring is called abhisheka. Then the bilva, laid on top, the leaf the Shiva Purana praises again and again in his worship.
And Shiva has a name for this: Ashutosha, which people explain as the one who is quickly pleased. The hunter's story is how the tradition shows it. He brought no devotion and no gift.
A few leaves and a little water, given by accident, and Shiva accepted them. How much more, the story asks, if you give them on purpose?

teach.h: A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.
teach.b: The Bhagavad Gita says something close, in Krishna's voice: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with devotion, is accepted. So the offering isn't a payment, and Shiva isn't a god you have to afford.
It's attention put into your hands. You pick the leaf, carry it, wait in line, and set it down with the name on your lips. Then the water runs off, the leaves are cleared away, and nothing is kept.

teach.h: YOU NEVER HAVE TO AFFORD HIM.
teach.b: You never have to wait until you have enough to come before God. A student with a plastic bottle of water stands in the same line as a family with a silver plate, and for Ashutosha, the water is enough.

how: On Maha Shivaratri, Hindus bring water, milk, bilva leaves and flowers to Shiva temples and offer them on the linga, sometimes waiting in line through the night; others offer them to a linga or image at home.

games.q: what does “maha shivaratri as a night curriculum” mean?
o: Shiva's night, when the costliest gift wins the most favor
Shiva's night, when offerings are kept on the altar all year
Shiva's night, when a leaf and water, given with care, are enough

p: leaves sacred to Shiva, three to a stem
explained as the one quickly pleased
leaves and water on a hidden linga

s: on this night Shiva's worship needs costly offerings
water, bilva leaves and wild flowers: nothing that costs much, so the care can be large.
in the Shiva Purana, the hunter meant to worship Shiva all along
he only wanted to hunt; leaves and water fell by accident, and Shiva still accepted them.
in the Gita, a leaf offered with devotion is accepted
Krishna names a leaf, a flower, a fruit and water.

games.q: you reach the shrine past midnight with nothing but a bottle of water. the person ahead of you has a full plate. what do you do?
o: leave; you've brought nothing worth giving.
pour your water slowly, with the name on your lips.
ask to borrow a few things from their plate.
games.why: Shiva is pictured as Ashutosha, quickly pleased. water given with care is the offering; what counts is how fully you put it down.

practice: Pour a little water into a cup if there's some nearby, or just rest your open hands in your lap, and think of the smallest thing you could give today: a minute of real listening, a kind word you've been holding back.
Hold it for a few breaths, then slowly put it down, as if setting a leaf on a stone. If you pray, you can offer it with Shiva's name, or the name of God you use.

wordCard.voice: Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva. Today's piece: the offering, water and bilva for Ashutosha, the one quickly pleased, given fully and let go.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bilva, the tree whose leaves are offered to Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: Ashutosha, Shiva is pleased by a leaf and water. The hunter gave by accident; you can give on purpose. Rest well.
